sections.overview: The white-lipped island pit viper is a venomous, fully tree-dwelling snake of Java and the Lesser Sunda Islands of Indonesia, and of Timor-Leste. It is related to the white-lipped pit viper of mainland Southeast Asia and is known for its colour forms, including a rare blue one.
sections.identification: A venom-study sample of adult snakes from eastern Java measured 40–69 cm in snout-to-vent length; this is a sample range, not a whole-body length or species maximum. The consulted sources do not report a reliable adult mass, width or sex-specific size comparison. There are three fairly distinct colour forms: green, found across the Lesser Sundas, blue, reported only on Komodo and Padar, and yellow, on Flores. The tail tip carries a conspicuous red stripe along its upper surface. The sources read give no body length, so none is stated.
sections.habitat: It occurs on Bali, Java, Flores, Lombok, Sumba, Sumbawa, Timor, Komodo and other islands, and in Timor-Leste, with the type locality at Soe on Timor. It generally stays in bushland and bamboo forest but sometimes enters inhabited areas in search of food.
sections.diet: It eats mice and lizards. A field naturalist suggested that skinks of the genus Sphenomorphus, very common on the islands he visited, probably make up much of its diet, but this is an inference, not a measurement.
sections.behavior: It is a fully arboreal snake, though one was seen crossing the forest floor at night on Komodo. It uses caudal luring, raising and wriggling its tail like a worm to attract prey. It is described as an aggressive predator that tends to stand its ground rather than flee.
sections.reproduction: The Reptile Database lists the species as ovoviviparous, meaning the eggs develop inside the female and she gives birth to live young. A field account notes that different colour forms can appear in the same litter. Litter size and breeding season were not found.
sections.ecology: As a predator of small lizards and rodents in island scrub and forest, it takes its place in local food webs. Its tail lure is the only hunting tactic described in the sources read. Its colour forms differ in abundance between islands for reasons that remain unclear.
sections.conservation: The Reptile Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. It is one of the most common causes of venomous snakebite on Bali, according to a magazine article citing an Australian Museum herpetologist; its haemorrhagic venom rarely kills but can cause severe swelling, tissue damage and bleeding. Its taxonomy is not settled across authors.
